title: Status Updates People Can Actually Act On
summary: A status update is a coordination tool. Lead with the ask, show evidence, name an owner, give a next-update time and say what readers don't need to do.
author: Nguyen Le Phong
html:
"Still in progress. The team is investigating. Will share next steps soon." Every word of that update is true. Nobody reading it can tell whether to wait, help, escalate or ignore it, so they do what people always do: send a private message asking "any news?"

A status update is a coordination tool. A good one cuts down the private pings, the repeated questions and the anxious guessing around a piece of work. It tells readers what changed and what, if anything, they should do about it. Teams that handle incidents for a living have practiced this under real pressure, and their habits carry over well to everyday project updates.

Borrow from incident response

In Google's incident model, one person takes the communication lead role and issues periodic updates to the response team and stakeholders, while the incident commander keeps a living incident document (Managing Incidents, from the Site Reliability Engineering book). PagerDuty's response guide asks its internal liaison for regular updates, roughly every 30 minutes, with an executive summary of the current status, and to "keep it short and to the point" (During an Incident).

My favorite detail comes from Atlassian's incident communication tutorial. Every template for an incident that's still open ends with "Next update in" and a time. Their note on it: you don't have to promise the fix will be working by then, you only need to tell people when they'll hear from you next (Incident communication tutorial). That one line heads off most "any update?" messages, because readers know when to look again.

Five parts of an update people can use

Updates people can act on usually have five parts: current state, evidence, blocker or risk, owner, and next step. Not every update needs all five spelled out, but when one is missing, readers have to guess it. Guessing is where confusion grows.

  • Current state, in words someone else can place on a map. "Almost done" is weaker than "deployed to staging, waiting on payment callback verification." "Investigating" is weaker than "checking whether retries doubled after the provider timeout."
  • Evidence: a test run, a log line, a screenshot, a PR link, a metric, a customer example. Without it, green can mean done, hopeful, or nobody has looked yet.
  • Blocker or risk, phrased as the action it needs. "Blocked by backend" is too wide. "Need Minh to confirm whether the new field is nullable before 15:00" is something Minh can do today.
  • Owner. An update without an owner is just a weather report. A name doesn't assign blame. It gives the follow-up somewhere to land.
  • Next step and next update: what happens next, and when readers will hear from you again.

Put the bottom line first

Military writers have a name for this: BLUF, short for bottom line up front. It comes from the US Army's correspondence regulation, AR 25-50, which makes putting the main point at the beginning one of the essentials of Army writing (BLUF). In a status update, the bottom line is usually one of three things: a decision you need, help you need, or "no action needed." Put it in the first line. Someone skimming a busy channel should get it even if they read nothing else.

Say what people don't need to do

Good updates draw boundaries too. "No customer action needed." "Please don't retry manually." "No release risk yet." "Escalate only if there's no callback by 17:00." Lines like these stop people from inventing work, such as a support lead drafting a customer apology for an issue that will never reach customers.

Before and after

Before

"Checkout issue: still investigating, will update soon."

After

"Checkout: need a decision from Lan by 14:00 on whether to turn off guest checkout for the rest of today. State: since 09:40, about 3% of card payments are timing out at the provider (dashboard link). Retries succeed for most of them. Owner: Huy. No customer action needed, and please don't retry orders by hand. Next update at 11:30, or sooner if the error rate passes 5%."

The second one is longer, and it saves everyone else time. Lan knows exactly what she has to decide and by when. Support knows to leave the orders alone. Everyone else knows when to look again, so nobody has to ping Huy in the meantime.

One test before you hit send

Ask yourself: after reading this, can someone decide, unblock or stop worrying? If not, the update may be true, but it isn't finished. If your updates keep producing decisions that then vanish in chat, a decision log is a good next habit, and Async Communication for Remote Teams covers the bigger picture.

Try this week

  • Open your next update with the ask, or with "no action needed."
  • Attach one piece of evidence to every status line: a link, a number, a log.
  • Rewrite one "blocked by X" as "need [person] to [action] by [time]."
  • End each update with the time of the next one.

faqs.q: What should a status update include?
faqs.a: Five parts cover most cases: the current state in concrete terms, evidence such as a link, log or metric, any blocker or risk phrased as the action it needs, a named owner, and the next step with the time of the next update. Put the decision or help you need in the first line.

faqs.q: How often should I send status updates?
faqs.a: Match the pace of change. During incidents, PagerDuty's guide asks for internal updates roughly every 30 minutes. For project work, daily or weekly is often enough. Whatever the rhythm, end each update with when the next one will come, so people don't have to ask.

faqs.q: How do I write a status update when there's no news?
faqs.a: Say what you checked, what you're doing next and when you'll update again. Atlassian's incident communication tutorial points out that you don't have to promise a fix by the next update, only tell people when they'll hear from you. 'Still working on it, next update at 15:00' is a useful message.

faqs.q: What does BLUF mean in a status update?
faqs.a: BLUF stands for bottom line up front, a writing rule from the US Army's correspondence regulation AR 25-50. In a status update it means the first line carries the decision you need, the help you need, or a clear 'no action needed', with the details below.
